title: At work: colleagues and routines
subtitle: opposite number, rapport, hot-desking, stuck in a rut
summary: Describe the people you work with and the rhythm of your working day, from establishing a rapport and taking the initiative to dead-end jobs and tight schedules.

lesson.heading: The people you work with
lesson.text: Your **opposite number** is the person who has the same position, or does the same job as you, in another office or company; the more formal equivalent is your **counterpart**. A good **working relationship** is your way of communicating and working together, and **collaboration** is working together to achieve shared goals.

examples.text: Philip is my **opposite number** in the company's New York office.
We have a good **working relationship** and there's a lot of day-to-day **collaboration**.
Having a **counterpart** like Philip in another branch is a great support.

lesson.heading: Bosses, rapport and hierarchy
lesson.text: A good boss quickly **establishes a rapport** with everyone - a warm, easy relationship - and likes staff to **take the initiative**, that is make decisions without being told what to do. A **hierarchical** company has a structure with important and less important people, and a **pecking order**: a system where some people have the right to get benefits or promotions before others.

examples.text: Last month we got a new boss, who quickly **established a good rapport** with everyone.
She likes us to **take the initiative**.
The company is very **hierarchical**; there's a **pecking order** for everything.

lesson.heading: How the office is organised
lesson.text: A **job-share** is an agreement where two people each share the same job. **Hot-desking** is a policy of sharing desks, so people sit at whichever desk is free on a particular day. **Workmates** are colleagues you are friendly with (informal, especially in non-professional jobs), and to **talk shop** is to talk about work outside work.

examples.text: I do a **job-share** with a woman called Rose, which suits us as we each have childcare responsibilities.
My office uses a **hot-desking** system, so I sit in a different place every day.
I socialise with my **workmates** outside of work, but we try not to **talk shop** on those occasions.

lesson.heading: Adjectives for describing a job
rows: makes you feel you have done something important, useful or well
encouraging new ideas or new thinking
you don't have to think about what you are doing
the same thing is repeated every day

lesson.heading: The working day
lesson.text: Your **workload** is the amount of work you have to do; it may be **heavy** or **light**. You **meet a deadline** when you finish something by a fixed day or time, and you **volunteer** when you offer to do something without being asked. Shift workers talk about the **day shift** and the **night shift**, and about **knocking off** - finishing work (informal).

examples.text: I'm really tired; I've had a very **heavy workload** recently.
Occasionally I have to **meet a deadline** or they need someone to **volunteer** for something.
All I ever think about is **knocking off** at three o'clock.
The shift I hate most is the **night shift**. I start at ten and work till six in the morning.

lesson.heading: Jobs you want to escape from
lesson.text: Some jobs have **irregular and antisocial hours** which do not let you have a normal social life. Others keep you **stuck behind a desk** all day, or run to very **tight schedules** - severely limited timetables. Worst of all is being **stuck in a rut**, trapped in a job you cannot escape from, or in a **dead-end job**, one with no prospects of promotion.

examples.text: I don't want an office job. I don't want to spend all day **stuck behind a desk**.
I'd hate to feel trapped in my job and to be **stuck in a rut**.
I stopped working in the hamburger restaurant. It was such a **dead-end job**.
We work to very **tight schedules**, and the hours are **irregular** and **antisocial**.

lesson.heading: Working for yourself
lesson.text: A **technician** does practical work with scientific or electrical equipment. If you **go in with** a friend you form a business partnership, perhaps as a **start-up** - a small business that has just started. Then you are **self-employed**. Someone who is **freelance** works for several different companies as and when they need work done.

examples.text: A friend suggested we set up a company together, so I **went in with** her and we formed a **start-up** in 2012.
I work for different companies at different times as it suits me. I'm **freelance**.
I used to work for someone else, but now I'm my own boss; I'm **self-employed**.

lesson.text: You take the initiative and you establish a rapport - neither collocation works with make.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence with the sentence that explains it.

pairs.right: There are several levels of management.
We do the same job but he's based in Rome.

pairs.left: We work to a tight schedule.
I don't think I'll be promoted before her.
pairs.right: There's a strict pecking order in the company.

exercises.prompt: I'm really tired; I've had a very heavy ___ recently.
exercises.hint: (the amount of work you have to do)
exercises.explanation: Your workload is the amount of work you have to do; it can be heavy or light.

exercises.prompt: I don't want an office job. I don't want to spend all day stuck ___ a desk.
exercises.explanation: To be stuck behind a desk is to sit at a desk all day (informal).

exercises.prompt: I'd hate to feel trapped in my job and to be stuck in a ___.
exercises.explanation: To be stuck in a rut is to be trapped in a job or situation you cannot escape from.

exercises.prompt: I work for different companies at different times as it suits me. I'm ___.
exercises.explanation: A freelance worker works for several different companies as and when they need work done.

exercises.prompt: I used to work for someone else, but now I'm my own boss; I'm ___.
exercises.explanation: If you work for yourself, you are self-employed.

exercises.prompt: I stopped working in the hamburger restaurant. It was such a dead-end ___.
exercises.explanation: A dead-end job is one with no prospects of promotion.

exercises.prompt: When I was working in the factory, all I could think of all day was the moment when I could knock ___.
exercises.explanation: To knock off is an informal way of saying to finish work.

exercises.prompt: I find ___ annoying, because it means I don't have my own desk where I can keep things at work.
exercises.explanation: Hot-desking is a policy of sharing desks, so people sit wherever is free that day.

exercises.prompt: A good friend suggested we set up a small company together, so I went in ___ her.
exercises.explanation: To go in with someone is to form a business partnership with them.

exercises.prompt: I think I have a good ___ relationship with my colleagues.
exercises.explanation: The fixed phrase is a good working relationship.

exercises.prompt: I tried to establish a good ___ with them from the very beginning.
exercises.explanation: You establish a rapport with someone - a report is a written document.

exercises.prompt: The person I like most is my opposite ___ in our office in Paris.
exercises.explanation: Your opposite number does the same job as you somewhere else in the company.

exercises.prompt: Being a hospital nurse is a good job, but you can't go out much with friends. The hours are a bit ___.
exercises.explanation: Antisocial (or irregular) hours do not let you have a normal social life.

exercises.statement: My boss likes me to make the initiative.
exercises.explanation: The verb is take: My boss likes me to take the initiative.

exercises.statement: I socialise with my jobmates outside of work.
exercises.explanation: The informal word is workmates: I socialise with my workmates outside of work.

exercises.statement: If a job is mind-numbing, it is extremely boring.
exercises.explanation: Correct - mind-numbing is a strong way of saying monotonous.

exercises.prompt: Does each adjective describe a boring job or an interesting one?
Put this sentence about an office system in order.
exercises.answer: My office uses a hot-desking system, so I sit in a different place every day
exercises.explanation: With hot-desking, people sit at whichever desk is free on a particular day.
